The Tui Chub Siphateles bicolor is a long-lived cyprinid endemic to the Great Basin, with a maximum recorded total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters]. This ultimate size is approached only by the largest individuals in lacustrine populations, as riverine fish rarely exceed 35 centimeters. Field surveys indicate that pubertal development is initiated when individuals reach a total length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters], a size typically attained during the second growing season. At a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the interval from fertilisation to hatching spans just 4 days , with chorion rupture occurring rapidly after the eyed stage. The protracted incubation period is followed by a yolk-dependent phase; the newly emerged alevin weighs approximately 0.0009 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0009 grams], reflecting the modest egg diameter of one to two millimeters. The transition to active feeding, marked by swim bladder inflation and mouth gape opening, is a critical period of high larval mortality.

Following eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains non-feeding until yolk absorption is complete, a process that takes 7 days at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], culminating in first exogenous feeding at 7 days after hatching [ab = 7 days after hatching]. This rapid exotrophic transition enables the prolarva to commence prey capture before its endogenous reserves are fully exhausted. In contrast, the total age from fertilisation to the onset of independent feeding is approximately 11 days. Growth during the larval period is allometric, with fin ray ossification and scale formation proceeding alongside a steady increase in body depth. The adult body mass corresponding to the ultimate total length has been estimated at 1,250 grams [Wwi = 1,250 grams], a value derived from a length–weight regression for lacustrine specimens. This substantial mass, coupled with an elongated lifespan, positions the Tui Chub as a relatively slow-growing species among western North American cyprinids.

Reproductive effort in Siphateles bicolor is modulated by seasonal temperature regimes. At a stable thermal environment of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], a gravid female measuring 37.8 centimeters in total length produces approximately 189 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 189 eggs per day], sustained over the protracted spawning period. This daily output, when integrated across the breeding season, represents a considerable investment in gamete production. Males typically attain puberty one year after birth [tp = one year after birth] under these same thermal conditions, whereas females require approximately two years after birth [tp = approximately two years after birth] to reach full gonadal maturity at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. The sexual dimorphism in maturation timing likely reflects the higher energetic demands associated with vitellogenesis and oocyte provisioning in females. Field observations indicate that spawning occurs from late spring through early summer, with multiple clutches produced by iteroparous adults over consecutive seasons.

Longevity records from mark-recapture studies and otolith analysis suggest that the maximum lifespan in the wild reaches three years [am = three years] when water temperatures average 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, combined with the delayed maturation of females, implies that most individuals spawn in only one or two breeding seasons before succumbing to senescence or predation. The age structure of natural populations is therefore dominated by young-of-the-year and one-year-old individuals, with older adults representing a diminishing fraction. Somatic growth decelerates markedly after the onset of reproductive activity, as resources are increasingly diverted toward gamete production. The species exhibits a type II survivorship curve, with constant mortality rates across age classes, a pattern consistent with its role as a forage fish in piscivore-dominated systems.

Comparative analyses reveal that the reproductive rate of Tui Chub is elevated relative to other Great Basin cyprinids of similar body size. At 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the combination of a high daily fecundity and an extended spawning window yields an annual output of approximately 189 eggs per day [Ri = 189 eggs per day] per female, with females producing roughly one clutch every two days over the summer months [F_R_i = roughly one clutch every two days over the summer months]. This output, which exceeds that of sympatric species such as the Lahontan redside, reflects an opportunistic life-history that capitalizes on ephemeral productivity pulses in shallow, warm lakes. The juvenile recruitment rate is density-dependent, with high larval mortality during the first week of exogenous feeding. Conservation efforts have focused on maintaining thermal refugia below 22 °C [T = 22 °C], as elevated temperatures accelerate developmental rates but also increase metabolic demand, potentially compressing the window for successful reproduction.
